findings.evidence: Line 23 addresses managers ('the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences') within instructions for employees. Lines 51-53 mix employee actions ('You record', 'You submit', 'You track') with backend process descriptions ('Finance reconciles', 'Payroll releases'), leaving unclear which sentences instruct the employee versus describe what staff does.
findings.fix: Separate backend process descriptions (Program Coordination, Review Responsibility) into a distinct section for internal/administrative audience. In How to Apply, remove manager-travel context or move it to a separate section on approval processes. In Terminology Notes, state upfront that 'You' sections address employees and separate finance/payroll descriptions into a distinct paragraph or section.
findings.location: How to Apply, paragraph 3 (line 23), and Terminology Notes section (lines 51-53)
findings.violation: The document addresses employees, managers, and backend staff (finance/payroll) within the same sections without clearly separating which instructions apply to which reader, making it unclear who should perform each action.

findings.evidence: Lines 10-11: 'If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.' The section opens with three conditional clauses before stating the governing rule (all conditions must be met).
findings.fix: Lead with the main rule: 'To qualify for the home-office equipment stipend, an employee must meet all three conditions: the position must count as full-time, the employee must have completed 90 days of continuous service, and the request must arrive before the benefit year ends.'
findings.violation: The main rule - that an employee must meet all three conditions simultaneously to qualify - is stated at the end after three separate conditions have accumulated, requiring re-reading to understand what actually qualifies someone.

findings.evidence: Eligibility precedes How to Apply (good sequence). However, Required Documentation (section 6) appears after Reimbursement Amounts (section 5), so employees read about dollar amounts before learning what documents they must provide. Restrictions and Exceptions (section 7) follows reimbursement details instead of appearing near or within Eligibility. Terminology Notes (section 8) and Request Steps (section 9) interrupt the workflow. A duplicate 'Overview' heading appears at line 59. Backend process sections (Program Coordination at line 63, Review Responsibility at line 67) are mixed with employee-facing content instead of grouped separately.
findings.fix: Reorganize sections in task order: Program Overview, Eligibility (with Restrictions and Exceptions), Required Documentation, How to Apply, Approval Timeline, Reimbursement Amounts, Request Steps. Move Terminology Notes and backend sections (Program Coordination, Review Responsibility) to an 'Administration' or 'For Staff' section at the end. Remove the duplicate Overview heading at line 59.
findings.location: Document structure as a whole, especially sections 6-12 (lines 31-73)
findings.violation: The section order does not follow the employee's actual task sequence: what can I apply for (Eligibility), what do I need to submit (Required Documentation), how do I submit it (How to Apply), what happens next (Approval Timeline), how much do I get (Reimbursement Amounts). Instead, Required Documentation appears after Reimbursement Amounts, and backend processes are scattered throughout.

findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: Lines 51-53: 'You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review. Also, you submit the request in the portal. You track its status there until the payment clears.' The section alternates between what the employee does ('You record', 'you submit', 'You track') and what backend staff does ('Finance reconciles', 'Payroll releases') without a signal explaining the theme or audience for each sentence.
findings.fix: Separate the section or add clear topic sentences: 'As an employee, you will: [employee actions]. Behind the scenes, the finance and payroll teams handle these steps: [backend actions].'
findings.violation: A reader finishing this section cannot name a single coherent theme; it appears to describe both employee tasks and backend processes without clarifying how they relate or which is being addressed.

findings.evidence: In Eligibility (lines 10-11), each of three sentences opens with a different condition ('If the position...', 'If the employee...', 'If the request...'), each introducing new information with no connection to the prior sentence. In How to Apply (line 23), the sentence 'Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email' suddenly shifts from employee instructions to manager/system context without connective text.
findings.fix: In Eligibility, reorganize to build on prior knowledge: 'To qualify, three conditions must all be met. First, the position must count as full-time. Second, the employee must have completed 90 days of continuous service. Third, the request must arrive before the benefit year ends.' In How to Apply, either remove the sentence about manager travel or set it apart as a separate note on approval process.
findings.location: Eligibility section, lines 10-11; How to Apply section, line 23
findings.violation: Sentences open with unrelated new information rather than building on what the reader has already learned, forcing re-orientation at each sentence boundary.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.

findings.evidence: The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist.
findings.fix: Replace the jargon term with a plain equivalent, or define it at first use.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a legal or foreign-language jargon term from the fixed list with no plain-language definition in the same or the following sentence.
